statute_title: Driving Under the Influence of Intoxicants
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first/second); Class C Felony (third+ within 10 years)
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle on premises open to the public or on a highway
While under the influence of intoxicating liquor, a controlled substance, an inhalant, or a combination
Or had a BAC of .08 or higher
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours jail or 80 hours community service (first); 48 hours (second)
enhancements: Third conviction within 10 years (Class C Felony)
notes: Oregon uses DUII (Driving Under the Influence of Intoxicants). Implied consent under ORS § 813.100. Admin license suspension 90 days (first BAC fail), 1 year (refusal). Diversion program available for first offense. Ignition interlock required.

penalty_min: 48 hours jail or 80 hours community service
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle on premises open to the public
While under the influence of intoxicants
BAC .08 or higher, or impairment of driving ability
No prior DUII convictions within 10 years
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours jail or 80 hours community service; 1-year license suspension
enhancements: BAC .15 or higher (enhanced minimum 48 hours jail, no community service option)
notes: DUII diversion program available for first offense under ORS § 813.200. Requires completion of treatment program and 1-year probation. Hardship permit available after 30 days.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (second); Class C Felony (third+ within 10 years)
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle while under the influence of intoxicants
BAC .08 or higher, or impairment of driving ability
One or more prior DUII convictions within 10 years
notes: Second offense: 3-year license revocation. Felony DUII: lifetime license revocation eligible. Ignition interlock required for all repeat offenders. No diversion for repeat offenders.

offense_class: Same as alcohol DUII by offense count
penalty_max: Same as alcohol DUII by offense count
fine_max: Same as alcohol DUII by offense count
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle on premises open to the public
While under the influence of a controlled substance, an inhalant, or a combination with alcohol
To a degree that impaired driving ability
mandatory_minimum: Same as alcohol DUII by offense count
enhancements: Combined influence of alcohol and drugs
Presence of Schedule I or II substance
notes: Oregon decriminalized possession of small amounts of hard drugs (Measure 110, 2020) but DUII remains fully criminal. No per se drug limit. Prosecution must prove impairment through DRE evaluation or other evidence.

elements: Defendant drove a vehicle on a highway or premises open to the public
Recklessly in a manner that endangered the safety of persons or property
notes: Common plea-down from DUII. Reckless driving is not a lesser included offense of DUII — separate elements. License suspension upon conviction.

statute_title: Failure to Perform Duties of a Driver — Injury
offense_class: Class C Felony (injury); Class A Misdemeanor (property damage)
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in injury to or death of any person
Defendant failed to perform the duties required under ORS § 811.700
enhancements: Death of victim (Class B Felony under § 811.705(2))
notes: Failure to perform duties when accident results in death is a Class B Felony. Duties include stopping, providing information, and rendering aid. Property damage only is a Class A Misdemeanor under § 811.700.

elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicants
Defendant recklessly caused the death of another person
notes: Oregon enacted aggravated vehicular homicide in 2007 specifically for DUII-related deaths. Also may be charged as manslaughter in the first degree (§ 163.118) or second degree (§ 163.125).

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
With criminal negligence
While operating a motor vehicle
notes: Oregon does not have a specific vehicular manslaughter statute. Vehicular deaths charged as criminally negligent homicide or manslaughter depending on culpability.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (violation level to felony depending on circumstances)
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a highway or premises open to the public
Defendant's driving privileges were suspended or revoked
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
notes: Driving while suspended for DUII is a Class C Felony (§ 811.182). Other suspensions are Class A Misdemeanor. Certain minor suspensions are violations only.

statute_title: Fleeing or Attempting to Elude a Police Officer
elements: A police officer in uniform gave a visual or audible signal to stop
Defendant willfully fled or attempted to elude the officer
The officer was operating an appropriately marked vehicle
notes: Always a Class C Felony in Oregon regardless of whether injury occurs. License revocation mandatory upon conviction.

offense_class: Class E Violation (small amounts under Measure 110); Class A or B Misdemeanor (larger amounts); Class C Felony (commercial quantities)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed
A controlled substance
Without a valid prescription or legal authorization
notes: Measure 110 (2020) decriminalized personal-use possession to a Class E Violation ($100 fine). However, Measure 110 was substantially rolled back in 2024 (HB 4002) recriminalizing possession as a misdemeanor. Current law: possession is Class A Misdemeanor with treatment court option.

offense_class: Violation (small amounts); Class B Misdemeanor (over limits); Class C Felony (commercial quantities)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed marijuana
In an amount exceeding the lawful limit
In a public place or without authorization
notes: Oregon legalized recreational marijuana in 2014 (Measure 91). Adults 21+ may possess up to 1 oz in public and 8 oz at home. Exceeding limits or possession by minors remains an offense.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed
Cocaine (Schedule II)
Without a valid prescription
notes: Originally a Class C Felony, reduced to violation under Measure 110, then recriminalized as misdemeanor under HB 4002 (2024). Treatment court option available.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed
Methamphetamine (Schedule II)
Without a valid prescription
notes: Recriminalized as misdemeanor under HB 4002 (2024) after Measure 110 decriminalization. Treatment court deflection option available. Manufacturing remains a serious felony.

statute_title: Unlawful Delivery or Manufacturing — Commercial Drug Offense
offense_class: Class A Felony (large quantities); Class B Felony (substantial quantities)
elements: Defendant knowingly manufactured, delivered, or possessed with intent to deliver
A controlled substance
In a quantity constituting a commercial drug offense
notes: Commercial drug offense thresholds defined in ORS § 475.900. Oregon uses delivery/manufacturing statutes rather than a single trafficking statute. Mandatory minimum sentences repealed under Measure 11 reform.

statute_title: Unlawful Delivery of a Controlled Substance
offense_class: Class B Felony (Schedule I-II); Class C Felony (Schedule III-V)
elements: Defendant knowingly delivered a controlled substance
To another person
Without legal authorization
notes: Delivery means actual, constructive, or attempted transfer. Oregon Measure 110 did not affect delivery/distribution charges. Substance-specific statutes exist (e.g., § 475.880 for heroin delivery).

statute_title: Unlawful Manufacturing of a Controlled Substance
offense_class: Class B Felony (Schedule I-II); Class C Felony (Schedule III-V)
elements: Defendant knowingly manufactured or attempted to manufacture
A controlled substance
Without legal authorization
enhancements: Manufacturing in presence of a minor
notes: Methamphetamine manufacturing (§ 475.886) carries enhanced penalties. Manufacturing marijuana in excess of legal limits is also covered. Cleanup costs assessed.

offense_class: Class C Misdemeanor (under 18); generally not prosecuted for adults under current law
elements: Defendant knowingly used or possessed with intent to use
Drug paraphernalia
For the purpose of using a controlled substance
enhancements: Delivery of paraphernalia to a minor
notes: Oregon largely decriminalized paraphernalia possession for adults. Delivery of paraphernalia (§ 475.525(2)) is a Class A Misdemeanor. Delivery to a minor is a Class C Felony.

offense_class: Class B Felony (Schedule I-II); Class C Felony (Schedule III-V)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed a controlled substance
With the intent to deliver to another person
Intent may be inferred from quantity, packaging, or other evidence
notes: Intent inferred from circumstantial evidence. Charged under the delivery statute. Same penalties as completed delivery.

penalty_max: Life with possibility of parole after 30 years; true life without parole for aggravated murder
elements: Defendant intentionally caused the death of another human being
With deliberate and premeditated malice
Or committed murder during certain felonies (felony murder)
enhancements: Aggravated murder (§ 163.095 — true life without parole)
Victim was a child, law enforcement officer, or other protected person
notes: Oregon does not have the death penalty (repealed 2022). Aggravated murder (§ 163.095) carries true life without parole. Measure 11 (1994) mandates minimum sentences for serious crimes.

elements: Defendant intentionally caused the death of another human being
Without premeditation (but with intent to kill)
Or committed homicide under circumstances of extreme indifference to human life
notes: Measure 11 mandatory minimum of 25 years. Oregon distinguishes intentional murder (with or without premeditation) from felony murder.

elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another human being
Under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life
Or committed a homicide under extreme emotional disturbance
notes: Extreme emotional disturbance (heat of passion) reduces murder to manslaughter. Measure 11 mandatory minimum of 10 years.

elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another human being
Or caused the death by criminal negligence
notes: Second degree manslaughter is Oregon's equivalent of involuntary manslaughter. Criminal negligence standard applies. Not a Measure 11 offense.

elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused serious physical injury to another
Or caused physical injury with a deadly weapon
Or recklessly caused serious physical injury with extreme indifference to human life
enhancements: Victim is a public safety officer
notes: Assault in the First Degree (§ 163.185) is a Class A Felony with a 90-month Measure 11 minimum. Second Degree is the more commonly charged aggravated assault.

elements: Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly caused physical injury to another person
enhancements: Domestic violence context (mandatory minimum jail time)
Against a public safety officer (Class C Felony)
notes: Assault 4 is Oregon's simple assault. Commonly charged in domestic violence situations. Against certain protected persons (emergency responders, transit workers) it becomes a Class C Felony.

elements: Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly caused physical injury to another person
notes: Oregon does not have a separate battery statute. Physical harm is prosecuted as assault in the fourth degree under § 163.160.

elements: Defendant took or attempted to take property from another person
By using or threatening the use of physical force
With intent to prevent resistance to the taking
notes: Third degree is the lowest robbery charge. Second degree (§ 164.405) involves aid of another or representation of being armed. First degree (§ 164.415) involves actual weapon or serious injury.

elements: Defendant committed robbery
While armed with a deadly weapon
Or caused or attempted to cause serious physical injury to another
notes: Measure 11 mandatory minimum of 90 months (7.5 years). No judicial departure or early release. One of the most serious property crimes.

elements: Defendant took another person from one place to another by unlawful force, threat, or deception
With intent to hold for ransom, terrorize, facilitate a felony, or cause physical injury
The victim was held in a place where likely to not be found
notes: Kidnapping in the Second Degree (§ 163.225) is a Class B Felony. First Degree (§ 163.235) requires additional aggravating circumstances. Measure 11 applies to first degree.

elements: Defendant intentionally started a fire or caused an explosion
That damaged a building which was occupied or reasonably likely to be occupied
enhancements: Fire set in wildland during fire season
notes: First degree arson requires occupied or likely-occupied building. Second degree (§ 164.315) covers unoccupied buildings. Oregon has additional reckless burning statutes (§ 164.335).

elements: Defendant intended to cause the death of another person
Defendant engaged in conduct constituting a substantial step toward the commission of murder
enhancements: Victim is a law enforcement officer
notes: Attempted murder is specifically listed as a Measure 11 offense with 90-month mandatory minimum. Attempted aggravated murder carries higher mandatory minimum.

statute_title: Assault in the Second Degree — With Deadly Weapon
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused physical injury to another
By means of a deadly or dangerous weapon
notes: Charged under Assault in the Second Degree. Measure 11 mandatory minimum of 70 months. Assault in the First Degree (deadly weapon + serious injury) carries 90-month minimum.

offense_class: Class C Felony (over $1,000); Class A Misdemeanor ($100-$1,000); Class C Misdemeanor (under $100)
penalty_max: 5 years (felony); 1 year (Class A Misd); 30 days (Class C Misd)
elements: Defendant committed theft of property of another
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Theft in the First Degree (§ 164.055) is over $1,000 — Class C Felony. Second Degree (§ 164.045) is $100-$1,000 — Class A Misdemeanor. Third Degree (§ 164.043) is under $100.

elements: Defendant committed theft of property
Value exceeded $1,000
With intent to deprive the owner
enhancements: Theft of a firearm (automatic first degree regardless of value)
notes: Oregon uses 'Theft in the First Degree' rather than 'grand theft.' Theft of a firearm, livestock, or explosives is automatically first degree regardless of value.

elements: Defendant committed theft of property
Value was under $100
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Lowest level theft. Under $100 is Theft 3 (Class C Misdemeanor). $100-$1,000 is Theft 2 (Class A Misdemeanor).

penalty_max: Same as general theft by value
fine_max: Same as general theft by value
elements: Defendant took merchandise from a retail establishment
Without paying the purchase price
With intent to deprive the merchant
enhancements: Organized retail theft (§ 164.098 — Class C Felony)
notes: Shoplifting charged under general theft statutes. Oregon enacted organized retail theft statute (§ 164.098) in 2023 to address large-scale retail theft.

elements: Defendant entered or remained unlawfully in a building
With intent to commit a crime therein
The building was a dwelling
Or defendant was armed, caused physical injury, or used a dangerous weapon
notes: First degree burglary is a Measure 11 offense with 70-month mandatory minimum. Must be a dwelling or involve additional aggravating factors. Second degree (§ 164.215) is a Class C Felony.

elements: Defendant entered or remained unlawfully in a dwelling
With intent to commit a crime therein
notes: All burglary of a dwelling is first degree in Oregon. Dwelling includes any building where a person habitually sleeps. Measure 11 mandatory minimum applies.

elements: Defendant took, operated, exercised control over, or otherwise used another's vehicle
Without consent of the owner
Knowing that the use was unauthorized
notes: Oregon has a specific unauthorized use of vehicle statute (§ 164.135), always a Class C Felony. May also be charged as Theft in the First Degree if permanent deprivation intended.

offense_class: Same classification as theft by value
elements: Defendant received, retained, or disposed of property of another
Knowing or having good reason to know the property was stolen
notes: Theft by receiving is classified the same as general theft based on value. Knowledge or reason to know stolen status must be proven.

offense_class: Class C Felony (over $1,000 or specific targets); Class A Misdemeanor ($100-$1,000); Class C Misdemeanor (under $100)
penalty_max: 5 years (felony); 1 year (Class A Misd); 30 days (Class C Misd)
elements: Defendant intentionally or recklessly damaged property of another
Without the owner's consent
notes: Criminal Mischief I (§ 164.365) is over $1,000 — Class C Felony. Criminal Mischief II (§ 164.354) is $100-$1,000 — Class A Misdemeanor. Criminal Mischief III (§ 164.345) is under $100.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first degree — dwelling); Class C Misdemeanor (second degree — other premises)
elements: Defendant entered or remained unlawfully upon premises
Knowing that the entry was unlawful
enhancements: Trespass in a dwelling (Criminal Trespass 1 — Class A Misdemeanor)
notes: Criminal Trespass in the First Degree (§ 164.255) involves a dwelling — Class A Misdemeanor. Second Degree (§ 164.245) covers other premises — Class C Misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant intentionally damaged or destroyed property of another
Or recklessly damaged property during the commission of a crime
notes: Three degrees: I (over $1,000 — Class C Felony), II ($100-$1,000 — Class A Misdemeanor), III (under $100 — Class C Misdemeanor).

statute_title: Assault in the Fourth Degree — Domestic Violence
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (basic); Class C Felony (strangulation or with certain priors)
elements: Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly caused physical injury
To a family or household member as defined in ORS § 135.230
enhancements: Prior domestic violence convictions (§ 163.160(3) — Class C Felony)
notes: Oregon uses 'domestic violence' as a designation on various crimes rather than a standalone offense. Strangulation statute (§ 163.187) enacted specifically for DV cases. Firearm prohibition upon conviction.

statute_title: Assault in the Fourth Degree — Domestic Violence (Physical Harm)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused physical injury to a family or household member
notes: Oregon does not have a separate domestic battery statute. Physical domestic harm is charged as Assault 4 with domestic violence designation.

statute_title: Endangering the Welfare of a Minor
elements: Defendant knowingly left a child unattended in a place or situation presenting substantial risk
Or failed to adequately supervise a child in a dangerous situation
enhancements: Drug manufacturing in presence of child (§ 163.547 — Class A Felony)
notes: Unlawful exposure to a controlled substance (§ 163.547) is a Class A Felony when a child is present during drug manufacturing. General endangerment is a misdemeanor.

statute_title: Criminal Mistreatment in the First Degree (Child Abuse)
offense_class: Class C Felony (first degree); Class A Misdemeanor (second degree)
elements: Defendant, being a person responsible for a dependent child
Intentionally or knowingly caused physical injury to the child
Or withheld necessary care creating a risk of physical injury
notes: Severe child abuse may be charged as Assault in the First or Second Degree with Measure 11 mandatory minimums. Criminal mistreatment covers both abuse and neglect.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class C Felony (subsequent within 5 years)
elements: A valid restraining or protective order was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant knowingly violated a term of the order
enhancements: Second or subsequent violation within 5 years (Class C Felony)
notes: Includes FAPA (Family Abuse Prevention Act) restraining orders, stalking protective orders, and elderly/disabled person protective orders.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class C Felony (subsequent or with protective order violation)
elements: Defendant knowingly engaged in repeated and unwanted contact
With another person or a member of that person's family
The person reasonably feared for their safety or the safety of a family member
enhancements: Violation of stalking protective order (Class C Felony)
notes: Two or more contacts sufficient. Contact includes following, appearing at workplace/home, and electronic communications. Stalking protective orders available under § 163.738.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (basic); Class A Misdemeanor (offensive physical contact); Class C Felony (repeat DV-related)
elements: Defendant intentionally harassed or annoyed another person
By subjecting the person to offensive physical contact
Or following the person in or about a public place
Or engaging in conduct that alarmed or coerced the victim
enhancements: DV-related with prior conviction (Class C Felony)
notes: Oregon harassment covers a broad range of conduct from offensive touching to threatening behavior. DV-designated harassment with prior DV conviction becomes a felony.

offense_class: Class C Felony (first degree); Class A Misdemeanor (second degree)
elements: Defendant, being a person responsible for a dependent elderly person
Intentionally or knowingly caused physical injury or withheld necessary care
Creating a risk of serious physical injury or death
notes: Criminal mistreatment covers both abuse and neglect of vulnerable adults. Financial exploitation of vulnerable persons (§ 163.705) is a separate Class C Felony.

elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
The defendant was a person prohibited from possessing firearms under § 166.250
enhancements: Possession of a loaded firearm in public
notes: Oregon Measure 114 (2022) imposed new permit-to-purchase requirements and magazine capacity limits, but enforcement has been stayed by courts. Concealed carry requires a concealed handgun license (CHL).

statute_title: Felon in Possession of a Firearm
offense_class: Class C Felony (most); Class B Felony (if prior person felony)
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
Defendant had a prior felony conviction
enhancements: Possession during commission of another crime
notes: Oregon classifies felon in possession as Class B Felony if the underlying felony was a person felony (violent crime). Federal 18 U.S.C. § 922(g) also applies.

statute_title: Unlawful Possession of a Firearm — Concealed Without License
elements: Defendant carried a concealed handgun
Without a valid Oregon concealed handgun license (CHL)
notes: Oregon requires a CHL for concealed carry. Open carry is generally legal except where prohibited by local ordinance. CHL issued by county sheriff. Measure 114 may impose additional restrictions if enforced.

statute_title: Unlawful Use of a Weapon (Reckless Discharge)
elements: Defendant recklessly discharged a firearm
In a manner that created a substantial risk of physical injury to another
notes: Unlawful use of a weapon is always a Class C Felony in Oregon. Includes pointing a firearm at another, even if unloaded. Celebratory gunfire prosecuted under this statute.

elements: Defendant, with intent to defraud
Obtained, possessed, transferred, or used personal identification of another
Without that person's authorization
enhancements: 10 or more victims (Aggravated Identity Theft under § 165.803 — Class B Felony)
notes: Aggravated identity theft (§ 165.803) involving 10+ victims is a Class B Felony. Oregon has a robust identity theft passport program for victims. Restitution required.

offense_class: Same classification as theft by value
elements: Defendant was entrusted with property by virtue of employment or position
Defendant knowingly converted the property to personal use
Without authorization
notes: Oregon does not have a separate embezzlement statute. Embezzlement is prosecuted as theft under the consolidated theft statutes (ORS Chapter 164).

offense_class: Class C Felony (first degree); Class A Misdemeanor (second degree)
elements: Defendant, with intent to injure or defraud
Falsely made, completed, or altered a written instrument
Or knowingly uttered a forged instrument
notes: Forgery in the First Degree (§ 165.013) involves instruments that evidence legal rights (money, securities, government documents). Second Degree (§ 165.007) covers other instruments.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Forged Instrument — Counterfeiting
elements: Defendant possessed a forged instrument
Knowing it to be forged
With intent to utter or deliver it
notes: Most currency counterfeiting is prosecuted federally. State charges cover counterfeit documents, identification, and other instruments. Charged under forgery statutes.

offense_class: Class C Felony (over $1,000); Class A Misdemeanor ($100-$1,000); Class C Misdemeanor (under $100)
elements: Defendant issued a check for the payment of money
Knowing it would not be honored by the drawee
With intent to defraud
notes: Same value thresholds as theft. Defendant must be given written notice and opportunity to make good before prosecution.

elements: Defendant knowingly presented or caused to be presented
A false or fraudulent claim or material misrepresentation
To an insurer for the purpose of obtaining payment
notes: Oregon Department of Consumer and Business Services investigates insurance fraud. Restitution and civil penalties also apply.

statute_title: Fraudulent Use of a Credit Card
elements: Defendant knowingly used a credit card or credit card number
Without authorization of the cardholder
To obtain property or services
notes: Oregon classifies credit card fraud as a Class C Felony regardless of amount. May also be charged as identity theft or theft by deception.

elements: Defendant knowingly engaged in a financial transaction
Involving proceeds of unlawful activity
With intent to promote criminal activity or disguise the nature or source of the proceeds
notes: Oregon enacted its own money laundering statute. Often charged alongside drug trafficking. Federal charges common for larger amounts. Asset forfeiture provisions apply.

offense_class: Same classification as theft by value
elements: Defendant obtained property of another by deception
By creating or reinforcing a false impression
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: General fraud prosecuted as theft by deception under Oregon's consolidated theft statutes. Value-based thresholds determine offense class.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual intercourse with another person
By forcible compulsion
Or the victim was under 12
Or the victim was incapable of consent by reason of mental defect, incapacitation, or physical helplessness
notes: Measure 11 mandatory minimum of 100 months (8+ years). Oregon does not have the death penalty. Lifetime sex offender registration required.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual intercourse with another person
Victim was under 14 and defendant was 3+ years older
notes: Rape in the Second Degree covers statutory rape of victims under 14. Rape in the Third Degree (§ 163.355) covers victims under 16 with defendant 3+ years older — Class C Felony.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (public indecency); Class C Felony (exposure to person under 13)
elements: Defendant exposed genitals in a public place
With intent of arousing sexual desire of the defendant or another
enhancements: Exposure to person under 13 (Class C Felony under § 163.467)
notes: Public indecency (§ 163.465) is a Class A Misdemeanor. Private indecency with person under 13 (§ 163.467) is a Class C Felony. May require sex offender registration.

elements: Defendant offered or agreed to pay a fee to engage in sexual conduct
Or solicited another to engage in prostitution
enhancements: Soliciting a minor (compelling prostitution — Class B Felony under § 167.017)
notes: Oregon decriminalized selling sex (prostitution) but maintained criminal penalties for buying (solicitation). Compelling prostitution of a minor is a Measure 11 offense.

offense_class: Class B Felony (Measure 11 — first degree); Class C Felony (second degree); Class A Misdemeanor (third degree)
penalty_max: 10 years (first degree); 5 years (second degree); 1 year (third degree)
elements: Defendant knowingly developed, duplicated, published, or possessed
A visual recording of sexually explicit conduct involving a child
Defendant knew or had reason to know the person depicted was a child
notes: Oregon uses 'Encouraging Child Sexual Abuse' rather than 'child pornography.' First degree (production) is a Measure 11 offense. Federal charges commonly apply.

statute_title: Failure to Register as a Sex Offender
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender
Defendant knowingly failed to register, report, or update registration
Within the time period required by law
notes: Must report within 10 days of establishing residence. Oregon classifies sex offenders into three levels for registration purposes. Failure to report is a separate felony.

statute_title: Rape — Victim Under Age of Consent
offense_class: Class C Felony (Rape 3, victim under 16); Class B Felony (Rape 2, victim under 14); Class A Felony (Rape 1, victim under 12)
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual intercourse with a minor below the age of consent
Defendant was at least 3 years older than the victim
notes: Age of consent is 18 in Oregon. Rape 3: victim under 16, defendant 3+ years older. Rape 2: victim under 14. Rape 1: victim under 12. Close-in-age exception for 3-year gap.

statute_title: Disorderly Conduct in the Second Degree
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm
Engaged in fighting or violent behavior
Or made unreasonable noise
Or obstructed vehicular or pedestrian traffic
enhancements: First degree (§ 166.023) if dangerous weapon involved (Class A Misdemeanor)
notes: Second Degree is Class B Misdemeanor. First Degree (§ 166.023) involves a weapon and is a Class A Misdemeanor. Commonly charged alongside other offenses.

elements: Defendant intentionally resisted a person known to be a peace officer
In making an arrest
notes: Resisting arrest is a Class A Misdemeanor. Does not require physical force — intentional obstruction is sufficient. But passive non-compliance alone may not qualify.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (obstructing); Class C Felony (hindering prosecution of felony)
elements: Defendant intentionally obstructed, impaired, or hindered
The administration of law or other governmental function
By means of intimidation, force, physical interference, or any independently unlawful act
enhancements: Hindering prosecution of a felony (Class C Felony under § 162.325)
notes: Obstructing governmental administration is a Class A Misdemeanor. Hindering prosecution (harboring fugitive, destroying evidence) is more serious — Class C Felony if the underlying crime is a felony.

offense_class: Remedial or punitive — up to 6 months per count for punitive contempt
elements: Defendant willfully disobeyed a lawful court order
Or engaged in conduct that obstructed the administration of justice
notes: Oregon distinguishes remedial contempt (to compel compliance) from punitive contempt (to punish). Due process protections apply. Jury trial right for serious contempt.

offense_class: Not a criminal offense (protective custody only)
elements: Person appeared intoxicated in a public place
Person was incapacitated or posed a danger to self or others
notes: Oregon decriminalized public intoxication. Intoxicated persons may be taken to a treatment facility or detox center, not jail. No criminal record. Oregon prioritizes treatment over criminalization.

statute_title: Failure to Appear in the First Degree
offense_class: Class C Felony (felony case); Class A Misdemeanor (misdemeanor case)
elements: Defendant was released on bail or personal recognizance
Defendant was required to appear in court at a specified time
Defendant knowingly failed to appear as required
notes: Failure to appear in a felony case is Failure to Appear 1 (Class C Felony). In a misdemeanor case, Failure to Appear 2 (§ 162.195 — Class A Misdemeanor). Bench warrant issued.

elements: Defendant knowingly initiated a false report or warning
Of an impending fire, explosion, crime, catastrophe, or emergency
Likely to cause public alarm or inconvenience
notes: Always a Class C Felony in Oregon. Includes false bomb threats, false 911 calls, and swatting. Defendant may be liable for costs of emergency response.

elements: Defendant, by word or conduct, intentionally attempted to place another person
In fear of imminent serious physical injury
enhancements: Use of a dangerous weapon (§ 163.190 — Class C Felony)
notes: Oregon uses 'menacing' rather than 'criminal threat.' Menacing with a dangerous weapon is Menacing (§ 163.190), a Class C Felony. Verbal threats alone may suffice if specific and imminent.

elements: Defendant made a false sworn statement
In an official proceeding
The statement was material
Defendant knew the statement was false
notes: False swearing (§ 162.075) outside official proceedings is a Class A Misdemeanor. Perjury requires materiality and an official proceeding. Corroboration or documentary evidence typically needed.

elements: Defendant offered, conferred, or agreed to confer a benefit
Upon a public servant
With the purpose of influencing the public servant's official action
notes: Both the giver and receiver may be charged. Oregon classifies bribery as a Class B Felony. Sports bribery (§ 162.035) is a Class C Felony.

offense_class: Class B Felony (first degree); Class C Felony (second degree); Class A Misdemeanor (third degree)
penalty_max: 10 years (first degree); 5 years (second degree); 1 year (third degree)
elements: Defendant escaped from custody
While in a correctional facility or during transport
enhancements: Use of physical force or weapon (first degree)
notes: Escape 1: using force, weapon, or from correctional facility. Escape 2: from custody without force. Escape 3: from less secure custody (work release, etc.). Sentence consecutive to original.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (animal abuse I); Class C Felony (aggravated animal abuse I)
elements: Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly caused physical injury to an animal
Or subjected an animal to cruel neglect
enhancements: Aggravated animal abuse (torture, mutilation) — § 167.322 (Class C Felony)
notes: Oregon has strong animal protection laws. Aggravated animal abuse (malicious torture, killing) is a Class C Felony. Animal fighting is separately criminalized. Forfeiture of animals ordered.

offense_class: Varies — court may revoke and impose sentence
penalty_max: Original sentence for the underlying offense
fine_max: Original fine for the underlying offense
elements: Defendant was placed on probation with specific conditions
Defendant violated one or more conditions of probation
notes: Court may continue, modify, or revoke probation. Oregon uses structured sanctions for technical violations. New criminal conduct typically leads to revocation. Hearing required.

offense_class: Varies — Board of Parole may revoke supervision
penalty_max: Remainder of supervision period (up to statutory maximum of original sentence)
elements: Defendant was released on post-prison supervision
Defendant violated one or more conditions of supervision
notes: Oregon uses 'post-prison supervision' rather than 'parole' for most offenders. Board of Parole and Post-Prison Supervision determines revocation. Structured sanctions for technical violations.

statute_title: Liability for Conduct of Another (Aiding and Abetting)
elements: Defendant aided or abetted another person
In planning or committing a criminal offense
With the intent to promote or facilitate the commission of the offense
notes: Oregon treats accomplices the same as principals. Mere presence at the scene is insufficient. Must have intent and take affirmative action to aid in the crime.

offense_class: One class below the target offense (except Measure 11 offenses)
penalty_max: Varies by class of the target offense
fine_max: Varies by class of the target offense
elements: Defendant intentionally engaged in conduct
Constituting a substantial step toward the commission of a crime
notes: Generally one class below the completed offense. Exception: attempted murder and other Measure 11 attempted offenses have specific mandatory minimums. Renunciation is a defense.

offense_class: One class below the target offense
penalty_max: Varies by class of the target offense
fine_max: Varies by class of the target offense
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to engage in conduct constituting a crime
Defendant or a co-conspirator performed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy
notes: One class below the target offense. Requires an overt act. Renunciation is a defense if the defendant prevents the commission of the crime. Conspiracy to commit a Class A Felony is a Class B Felony.
